title: User-defined dynamical systems
text: Duffing oscillator one studied examples nonlinear dynamics [5]. Named Georg Duffing, first analyzed 1918, equation describes damped oscillator nonlinear restoring force [8]: \[\ddot{x} + \delta \dot{x} + \alpha x + \beta x^3 = \gamma \cos(\omega t)\] : \(\delta\) damping coefficient \(\alpha\) controls linear stiffness (negative double-well potential) \(\beta\) nonlinear stiffness parameter \(\gamma\) forcing amplitude \(\omega\) forcing frequency Converting first-order system \(v = \dot{x}\): \[\begin{aligned} \frac{dx}{dt} &= v \\ \frac{dv}{dt} &= -\delta v - \alpha x - \beta x^3 + \gamma \cos(\omega t) \end{aligned}\] potential energy function : \[V(x) = \frac{\alpha}{2}x^2 + \frac{\beta}{4}x^4\] \(\alpha < 0\) \(\beta > 0\), creates double-well potential stable equilibria \(x = \pm\sqrt{-\alpha/\beta}\) unstable saddle \(x = 0\). presence external forcing can lead chaotic behavior fractal basin boundaries [9].

text: Henon map [6] discrete-time dynamical system introduced Michel Henon 1976 simplified model Poincare section Lorenz system. defined : \[\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= 1 - x_n^2 + y_n \\ y_{n+1} &= b x_n \end{aligned}\] : \(\) controls nonlinearity (typically \(= 1.4\)) \(b\) dissipation parameter (typically \(b = 0.3\)) Jacobian determinant \(\det(J) = -b\), making dissipative map \(|b| < 1\). classical parameters \((, b) = (1.4, 0.3)\), map exhibits strange attractor fractal dimension approximately \(1.26\) [11]. fixed points found solving \(x = 1 - ax^2 + bx\) \(y = bx\): \[x^* = \frac{(1-b) \pm \sqrt{(1-b)^2 + 4a}}{2a}\]

title: User-defined dynamical systems
text: Van der Pol oscillator [7][12] non-conservative system nonlinear damping, introduced Balthasar van der Pol 1926 describe oscillations vacuum tube circuits. equation : \[\ddot{x} - \mu(1 - x^2)\dot{x} + x = 0\] \(\mu > 0\) nonlinearity parameter. key feature : \(|x| < 1\): negative damping (energy input) \(|x| > 1\): positive damping (energy dissipation) creates self-sustained oscillation stable limit cycle. period oscillation increases \(\mu\): \[T \approx (3 - 2\ln 2)\mu + O(\mu^{-1/3}) \quad \text{} \mu \gg 1\] external forcing added [13]: \[\ddot{x} - \mu(1 - x^2)\dot{x} + x = \cos(\omega t)\] system can exhibit complex behavior including frequency entrainment, quasiperiodic motion, chaos [14]. Converting first-order form \(v = \dot{x}\): \[\begin{aligned} \frac{dx}{dt} &= v \\ \frac{dv}{dt} &= \mu(1 - x^2)v - x + \cos(\omega t) \end{aligned}\]

title: Wada basins: mathematical foundations and computational detection
text: dynamical system mathematical formalization deterministic rule describes point geometric space evolves time. Formally, consider phase space \(\mathcal{M} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), set possible states system, \(d\) denotes dimension state space (.e., number variables needed completely specify system’s state). evolution system governed flow \(\phi: \mathbb{R} \times \mathcal{M} \\mathcal{M}\), continuous mapping satisfying: Identity: \(\phi(0, x) = x\) \(x \\mathcal{M}\) Group property: \(\phi(t + s, x) = \phi(t, \phi(s, x))\) \(t, s \\mathbb{R}\) \(x \\mathcal{M}\) write \(\phi_t(x) := \phi(t, x)\) denote state time \(t\) starting initial condition \(x\). flow typically generated ordinary differential equation (ODE): \[\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, t)\] \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_d)^{\top} \\mathcal{M}\) state vector \(\mathbf{f}: \mathcal{M} \times \mathbb{R} \\mathbb{R}^d\) vector field defining dynamics. autonomous systems, \(\mathbf{f}\) depend explicitly time: \(\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\).

text: compare slim boundaries quantitatively, method uses Hausdorff distance, metric space compact subsets. Definition: two non-empty compact sets \(X, Y \subset \mathbb{R}^d\), Hausdorff distance : \[d_H(X, Y) := \max\left\{ \sup_{x \X} d(x, Y), \sup_{y \Y} d(y, X) \right\}\] \(d(x, Y) := \inf_{y \Y} \|x - y\|\) distance point \(x\) set \(Y\). Equivalently: \[d_H(X, Y) = \inf\{\varepsilon > 0 : X \subseteq Y^\varepsilon \text{ } Y \subseteq X^\varepsilon\}\] \(X^\varepsilon := \{z : d(z, X) < \varepsilon\}\) \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood \(X\). Wada criterion: Compute \(d_H(\partial_i, \partial_j)\) pairs \((, j)\). maximum pairwise distance, normalized phase space diameter \(D\), threshold: \[\frac{\max_{\neq j} d_H(\partial_i, \partial_j)}{D} < \tau\] (typically \(\tau = 0.1\) \(0.05\)), basins declared Wada.

text: Let \(\mathcal{M} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) denote phase space dynamical system, let \(\phi_t: \mathcal{M} \\mathcal{M}\) represent time-evolution operator (flow map), \(\phi_t(x)\) denotes state system time \(t\) given initial condition \(x \\mathcal{M}\). assume system possesses finite collection disjoint, asymptotically stable compact invariant sets, termed attractors, denoted \(\{A_1, \ldots, A_{N_A}\}\). basin attraction \(B_i\) associated attractor \(A_i\) defined set initial conditions \(x \\mathcal{M}\) whose trajectories asymptotically approach \(A_i\) time tends infinity. Formally: \[B_i = \lbrace x \\mathcal{M} : \lim_{t \\infty} \text{dist}(\phi_t(x), A_i) = 0 \rbrace\] \(\text{dist}(y, ) = \inf_{z \} \|y - z\|\) represents minimum Euclidean distance point \(y\) set \(\). Let \(\partial S\) denote topological boundary set \(S\), defined \(\partial S = \overline{S} \setminus \text{int}(S)\), \(\overline{S}\) closure \(\text{int}(S)\) interior \(S\). collection basins \(\{B_1, \ldots, B_{N_A}\}\) said possess Wada property system least three attractors (\(N_A \geq 3\)) boundaries basins identical: \[\partial B_1 = \partial B_2 = \cdots = \partial B_{N_A} = \mathcal{J}\] \(\mathcal{J}\) common boundary set (invariant set). direct topological consequence property every point \(x \\mathcal{J}\) boundary, open neighborhood \(U_\epsilon(x)\) radius \(\epsilon > 0\) centered \(x\) must non-empty intersection every basin: \[U_\epsilon(x) \cap B_i \neq \emptyset, \quad \forall \\{1, \ldots, N_A\}\] implies state initialized infinitesimal uncertainty boundary \(\mathcal{J}\) non-zero probability evolving toward \(N_A\) attractors.

text: Define systems compiled_system(). canonical route accepts janos::model_spec object via model argument: dynamics written R formulas, internal adapter calls janos::model_spec_rhs_cpp() inline per-state right-hand sides OpenMP basin kernel. example builds bistable forced Duffing oscillator, computes basins 300x300 grid, applies Wada detection, renders result.  users without janos installed, ad-hoc kernel snippets preferred formula-based specification, compiled_system() also accepts dynamics raw C++ string state[] bare-parameter conventions basin template: two routes produce numerically identical compiled objects.
code: # Bistable forced Duffing oscillator as a janos model_spec duffing_spec <- janos::model_spec(     rhs = list(         x ~ y,         y ~ -delta * y - alpha * x - beta * x^3 + gamma_f * cos(omega * t)     ),     state_names = c("x", "y"),     parms = list(delta = 0.3, alpha = -1, beta = 1, gamma_f = 0.5, omega = 1.2) )  # Adapt to wadaR's basin kernel (OpenMP-parallel, numerically identical # to the raw cpp_dynamics route) duffing <- compiled_system(     model      = duffing_spec,     attractors = list(         attractor_point(c( 1, 0), 0.3, "right well"),         attractor_point(c(-1, 0), 0.3, "left well"),         attractor_point(c( 0, 0), 0.3, "origin")     ),     name    = "Duffing oscillator (from janos model_spec)",     verbose = FALSE )  # Compute basins and apply Wada diagnostics basins      <- compute_basins(duffing, c(-2, 2), c(-2, 2),                               resolution = 300, verbose = FALSE) entropy     <- basin_entropy(basins) grid_result <- wada_grid_method(basins) #> ¡ Basin matrix: 300 x 300, 3 attractors #> ⚙ Grid method: 300x300 grid, 3 attractors #> ¡ Classifying boundary boxes (parallel Rcpp, 19 cores)... #> ⏱ Classification: 0.00 seconds #> ¡ Refining 18881 boundary boxes with ODE bisection (parallel Rcpp, 19 cores)... #> ¡ Press Esc to abort computation #> ⏱ Refinement: 139.61 seconds #> ¡ Results: #>   G_2: 10973 boxes (W_2 = 0.4252) #>   G_3: 14836 boxes (W_3 = 0.5748) #> ⚠ Basin is PARTIALLY WADA or NOT WADA  plot(basins,      title  = "Duffing basins specified via janos::model_spec()",      colors = palettes(palette = "okabe_ito")[1:3]) duffing <- compiled_system(     cpp_dynamics = '         deriv[0] = state[1];         deriv[1] = -delta * state[1] - alpha * state[0]                    - beta * state[0] * state[0] * state[0]                    + gamma_f * cos(omega * t);     ',     attractors = list(         attractor_point(c( 1, 0), 0.3, "right well"),         attractor_point(c(-1, 0), 0.3, "left well"),         attractor_point(c( 0, 0), 0.3, "origin")     ),     dim = 2, type = "ode",     params = list(delta = 0.3, alpha = -1, beta = 1, gamma_f = 0.5, omega = 1.2),     name = "Duffing oscillator" )

title: Compute basin entropy — basin_entropy
text: Mathematical background: basin entropy, introduced Daza et al. (2016), measures unpredictability dynamical system's final state given uncertainty initial condition. grid divided boxes size \(\epsilon\), entropy box \(\) : $$S_i = -\sum_{j=1}^{N_A} p_{ij} \log_b(p_{ij})$$ \(p_{ij}\) fraction box \(\) belonging basin \(j\), \(N_A\) number attractors, \(b\) logarithm base. total basin entropy average boxes: $$S_b = \frac{1}{N_{box}} \sum_{=1}^{N_{box}} S_i$$ Interpretation: \(S_b = 0\): boxes monochromatic (uncertainty) \(S_b = \log_b(N_A)\): Maximum uncertainty (uniform distribution boxes) Wada basins, \(S_b\) approaches \(\log_b(N_A)\) boundary, boundary boxes contain \(N_A\) basins fine scales. Boundary basin entropy: boundary basin entropy \(S_{bb}\) considers boxes intersecting basin boundary. focuses unpredictability boundary structure, relevant Wada basins. true Wada basins, \(S_{bb}\) approach \(\log_b(N_A)\).

title: Compute Hausdorff distance between two point sets — hausdorff_distance
text: Hausdorff distance defined maximum directed Hausdorff distances directions: $$d_H(X, Y) = \max\{\vec{d}_H(X, Y), \vec{d}_H(Y, X)\}$$ directed Hausdorff distance : $$\vec{d}_H(X, Y) = \sup_{x \X} \inf_{y \Y} \|x - y\|$$ Intuitively, \(d_H(X, Y)\) minimum radius \(r\) every point \(X\) within distance \(r\) point \(Y\), vice versa. Properties: Hausdorff distance satisfies \(d_H(X, Y) \geq 0\) (non-negativity), \(d_H(X, Y) = 0\) iff \(X = Y\) (identity indiscernibles), \(d_H(X, Y) = d_H(Y, X)\) (symmetry), \(d_H(X, Z) \leq d_H(X, Y) + d_H(Y, Z)\) (triangle inequality). Implementation: function uses efficient C++ implementation O(n log m + m log n) complexity. large point sets, consider subsampling.

title: Detect Wada basins using the grid method — wada_grid_method
text: Mathematical background: Consider dynamical system \(N_A \geq 3\) attractors. initial condition \(\mathbf{x}_0\) belongs exactly one basin attraction \(B_k\), \(k = 1, \ldots, N_A\). basins Wada property every point boundary one basin simultaneously boundary basins: $$\partial B_1 = \partial B_2 = \cdots = \partial B_{N_A}$$ grid method algorithm: grid \(n \times n\) boxes, define box \(B_i\): $$m_i = \text{number distinct basins neighborhood } B_i$$ algorithm proceeds follows: Classify grid box number distinct basins 8-connected neighborhood (Moore neighborhood) Identify boundary boxes \(1 < m_i < N_A\) boundary box, construct segment nearest box different basin Apply bisection refinement find additional basins along segment Update \(m_i\) based discovered basins Classification statistics: algorithm computes: $$G_m = |\{: m_i = m\}| \quad \text{(number boxes bordering } m \text{ basins)}$$ $$W_m = \frac{G_m}{\sum_{j>1} G_j} \quad \text{(proportion boundary boxes)}$$ Wada criterion: basin classified Wada \(W_{N_A} \approx 1\), meaning boundary boxes border \(N_A\) basins. implementation uses: $$\text{\_wada} = (W_{N_A} > 1 - \text{tolerance})$$ Computational complexity warning: grid method runtime depends number boundary boxes refinement depth. high-resolution grids (>400x400) many boundary points, computation can slow. parameter max_refinements controls maximum bisection depth; reducing speeds computation cost accuracy. Use max_refinements = 10 quick screening, max_refinements = 20 (default) accurate results, large grids consider using wada_merging_method first quick screening.

text: Mathematical background: Consider dynamical system \(N_A\) basins attraction \(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_{N_A}\). Wada property states : $$\partial B_1 = \partial B_2 = \cdots = \partial B_{N_A}$$ key insight basins Wada property, merging subset basins change common boundary. Specifically, basin \(B_i\), define merged basin: $$M_i = \bigcup_{j \neq } B_j$$ boundary \(B_i\) \(M_i\) called slim boundary. Wada basins, slim boundaries identical: $$\partial(B_1, M_1) = \partial(B_2, M_2) = \cdots = \partial(B_{N_A}, M_{N_A})$$ merging algorithm: basin \(B_i\) (\(= 1, \ldots, N_A\)): Merge basins \(M_i\) Extract slim boundary \(\partial_i\) \(B_i\) \(M_i\) Compute Hausdorff distance pairs slim boundaries Analyze distance matrix determine Wada property Hausdorff distance: Hausdorff distance point sets \(X\) \(Y\) : $$d_H(X, Y) = \max\{\sup_{x \X} d(x, Y), \sup_{y \Y} d(y, X)\}$$ \(d(x, Y) = \inf_{y \Y} \|x - y\|\) distance point \(x\) set \(Y\). title: Detect Wada basins using the saddle-straddle method — wada_straddle_method
text: Mathematical background: dissipative dynamical systems \(N_A \geq 3\) coexisting attractors, basin boundaries contain chaotic saddle \(S\)—invariant set trajectories exhibit chaotic behavior eventually escaping attractor. Wada property implies single connected chaotic saddle lying basin boundaries simultaneously: $$S = S_1 = S_2 = \cdots = S_{N_A}$$ \(S_i\) chaotic saddle boundary basin \(B_i\) merged basin \(M_i = \bigcup_{j \neq } B_j\). saddle-straddle algorithm: algorithm approximates chaotic saddle : Find segment straddling boundary (endpoints different basins) Use bisection refinement segment length \(< \varepsilon\) Record midpoint (approximately saddle) Iterate endpoints forward time (segment expands along unstable manifold saddle) segment length exceeds threshold, refine repeat Continue desired number saddle points collected key insight points chaotic saddle repel trajectories exponentially fast along unstable manifold, causing straddling segment stretch. Repeated bisection converges saddle. Wada criterion: Compute Hausdorff distance pairs computed saddles. basins Wada : $$d_H(S_i, S_j) \ll \text{diam}(S)$$ \(\text{diam}(S)\) diameter saddle set. implementation uses threshold \(d_H < 0.01 \cdot \text{diam}\). Computational complexity warning: computationally expensive Wada detection method. \(N_A\) merged basin pairs, algorithm must find initial straddling points via random sampling, integrate two trajectories forward collecting saddle points, perform repeated bisection refinements. total number ODE integration steps scales approximately \(O(N_A \times n\_points \times T/\Delta t)\). 3 basins n_points=10000, can take several minutes hours. Use n_points = 1000-2000 exploration, increase n_points = 5000-10000 accurate saddle approximation, consider using wada_grid_method wada_merging_method faster Wada detection dynamical insight needed.
